note: Registrar-log vectors (§2). `log` cases verify one copy of a log under a pinned key; `network` cases assemble the world from pins and the delegations their logs name, then resolve; `discovery` cases read `_nomos-registrar` TXT records. Every expect is written from the specification text. Generated by generate_registrar_logs.py, byte-identical on every run.

cases.description: A genuine log under an Ed25519 key: chain from 64 zeros, head signed for this log's name.
A genuine log under a P-256 key held in an HSM: the suite is ES256 because the key is P-256 (§2.1).
A head that omits its `log` field still verifies: the log name is inside the signed payload.
A head the same key signed for another registrar's log (qfc), presented as the DIFC's: its `log` names the other log.
The same replay with the `log` field stripped: the signature covers the other log's name, so it fails here.
A P-256 key's head that names Ed25519: the key fixes the suite, never the head (§2.1).
A P-256 key's head that names WebAuthn-ES256, a weaker framing: refused, the key verifies ES256 only.
A head signed by another key under its own kid: not the key the relying party pinned.
A head naming the pinned kid, signed by another key.
An ES256 head signature with a high S value: SPEC-010 refuses it.
The DIFC rotates from its P-256 key to an Ed25519 key with a `key` entry its old key signed; a relying party pinned to the old key follows it (§2.2).
A relying party that pins the new key: the walk starts after the entry that introduced it.
After a rotation, a head still signed by the old key: the key in force is the new one.
A `key` entry the key in force did not sign, appended to hand the log to an attacker's key, with a head the attacker signed: the whole log is refused.
A head kept from an earlier read that this copy of the log does not contain: history was rewritten.
A head kept from an earlier read, extended by today's log.
A head signed an hour before now, past the relying party's 600 s bound.
An entry altered after it was chained: its hash no longer matches its contents.
A head naming more entries than the copy holds.

The pinned platform registrar recognizes the DIFC's own registrar for acts by DIFC establishments, naming its P-256 key and log. The DIFC's log is fetched, verified under that key and folded as a delegate; on a DIFC act its law is resolved.
The same world on an act in the UAE by a mainland firm: the edge is FALSE, the DIFC's law is not walked, and the UAE's law is resolved.

The DIFC's log is served with a head an attacker signed under its own key: not the key the recognizing entry named. The delegate is left out, and a DIFC act is INCOMPLETE naming it, never resolved without its law.
The DIFC's log cannot be fetched. A DIFC act is INCOMPLETE naming the DIFC registrar; an act it does not reach is unaffected.
Two pinned registrars recognize the same delegate under different keys. The resolver does not choose: the delegate is left out, and a DIFC act is INCOMPLETE.
The DIFC rotated its key after it was recognized. The recognizing entry still names the old key; the rotation, signed by that key, is followed.
With a bound of one recognition hop, a registrar two hops from the pin is not read: it is beyond bounds, and a resolution that walks to it is INCOMPLETE naming it.

The platform registrar withdrew its recognition of the DIFC registrar. The delegate is not fetched and not walked, and on a DIFC act the platform's own law does not apply: RESOLVED with no law, under the platform's closure. This is why a registrar hands law over by recognizing first and withdrawing its own claim after, never the reverse.
The record names the registrar and the kid already held: its URL is where the log is read.
Unrelated TXT records at the same name are skipped.
A spoofed record naming an attacker's kid: DNS never supplies a key, and a record that disagrees with the held kid refuses the registrar.
A record for another registrar id.
A record pointing at plain http.
A record without a kid is not a record.
A record of another version is not a record.
